title: Green Potatoes: Why They Turn Green and When Not to Eat Them

seo.title: Are Green Potatoes Safe to Eat?
seo.meta_description: Green color is chlorophyll, but light exposure can also increase potato glycoalkaloids. Learn why green potatoes are best discarded.
seo.search_intent: Food safety explanation of green potatoes.

excerpt: The green pigment itself is harmless chlorophyll, but greening signals light exposure that can also raise glycoalkaloids such as solanine and chaconine. EFSA's consumer guidance says green potatoes should not be eaten.
content_html:
A green potato has produced chlorophyll after light exposure. Chlorophyll is not the toxin. The concern is that the same stress can increase natural potato defense compounds called glycoalkaloids.

Green is a warning signal, not a glycoalkaloid meter

Greenness does not tell you an exact solanine concentration. Some non-green potatoes can contain glycoalkaloids too. But visible green tissue is a practical sign that storage conditions favored unwanted changes.

Should you just cut the green part away?

Peeling can reduce glycoalkaloids because they are concentrated near the skin. EFSA consumer guidance nonetheless advises not eating green potatoes. That avoids pretending a home cook can measure the starting concentration.

Cooking is not a reliable rescue method

EFSA reports broad reductions from peeling, boiling and frying, but the ranges are too variable to guarantee a particular green potato has been made safe.

Possible symptoms

High glycoalkaloid intake can cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. Bitter taste and oral burning can be warning signs, but do not taste-test a suspicious potato.

Prevent greening

Store potatoes cool, dry, ventilated and protected from light. Do not keep them for days in direct sunlight or under strong kitchen lights.

Frequently asked questions

Is the green part solanine?

No. It is chlorophyll, but it can indicate conditions that also raise glycoalkaloids.

Can peeling make a green potato safe?

Peeling reduces glycoalkaloids but does not let you know the remaining amount; EFSA consumer guidance says not to eat green potatoes.

Does frying destroy solanine?

It can reduce glycoalkaloids variably, but not with enough predictability to rescue a clearly green potato.

faq.question: Is green potato color itself toxic?
faq.answer: No. The green is chlorophyll, but it signals light exposure that can coincide with increased glycoalkaloids.

faq.question: Should green potatoes be eaten after peeling?
faq.answer: EFSA consumer guidance advises against eating green potatoes.

faq.question: Can cooking make a green potato safe?
faq.answer: Processing can reduce glycoalkaloids but the reduction is variable and not a reliable home safety guarantee.
